# A layout that tells the truth {#sec-layout}

A repository should show its boundaries before a reader opens a file. Keep application code,
reusable code, tests, and build helpers in predictable places.

## A conventional top level {#sec-pitchfork}

The [Pitchfork layout](https://joholl.github.io/pitchfork-website/) is a useful C++ reference,
not a standard. Sketchbook adapts the idea to keep the application and its separable library
side by side:

```text
qt-kickstart/
├── CMakeLists.txt       project and dependencies
├── CMakePresets.json    shared build configurations
├── cmake/               build helpers
├── docs/                this guide
├── external/            third-party sources
├── libs/                separable libraries
├── src/                 application features
└── tests/               application tests
```

Pitchfork distinguishes a single `src/` layout from a `libs/` layout. This project combines
them: `src/` holds the app, while `libs/shapes/` can stand alone with its own tests.

## Public API is a promise {#sec-include-dirs}

A library's public headers are the contract other code may include. Keep them under
`include/<name>/`; keep implementation headers beside the source. Consumers normally do not
need to depend on a private detail.

A small public API gives a library room to change. Once consumers rely on a declaration,
changing it can require them to update or rebuild their code. A distributed binary library
may also promise that existing compiled consumers continue to work. Keep implementation
details private so that promise covers only what consumers actually need.

::: {.snippet source="libs/shapes/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
add_library(shapes STATIC)
        FILES include/shapes/Recognizer.h\n)
```

:::

A feature inside one application does not need to pretend it is a library. Keep its QML and
C++ together until another application needs the code.

The extra `shapes/` directory in the public include path makes `#include <shapes/Recognizer.h>`
identify its library and avoids collisions with another library's `Recognizer.h`. Private
headers remain implementation details, but a directory layout alone cannot prevent someone
from reaching into them. The build's target dependencies support the boundary.

## Names make ownership clear {#sec-namespaces}

Put library code in the library namespace and application code in `app::<feature>`. Namespaces
stop collisions and make an unfamiliar type easier to place. Keep helpers in an unnamed
namespace in a `.cpp` file. Never put `using namespace` in a header.

Macros do not follow C++ namespaces. Prefer a constant or function where possible, or give a
macro a project-specific prefix. For types exposed through Qt's meta-object system, spelling
names fully qualified in properties, signals, and invokable signatures also helps the QML tools
identify them correctly.

## Feature folders keep change local {#sec-features}

Put the parts that change together in one feature folder: QML, C++ state, and the feature's
CMake target. Sketchbook puts its canvas, notebook, and controls in separate folders. Its
tests mirror that shape, so a test is easy to find.

## Small libraries earn their boundary {#sec-separable}

Move code to `libs/` when it can live without the application. Sketchbook's recognizer is
plain C++, has its own public header and tests, and has no QML dependency. A library may use
Qt when Qt belongs in its public design.

## Include hygiene {#sec-include-style}

Each source file should include the declarations it uses instead of depending on another
header to include them by accident. Group the file's own header first, then project headers,
third-party headers, and standard library headers. For Qt headers, including by module, such
as `<QtCore/QObject>`, makes the dependency visible to a reader.

## Include only what a declaration needs {#sec-forward-declarations}

Include a base class, a value member, and types used by inline code. Forward-declare a type
that appears only as a pointer or reference. This keeps a public header smaller and avoids
pulling an implementation dependency into every consumer.

An owning pointer such as `std::unique_ptr<SomeType>` can use a forward declaration too. Its
owning class must define the destructor where `SomeType` is complete, typically in the source
file. That is where the pointer actually deletes its object.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Detail: private implementation and binary compatibility

Qt's private headers use a separate private API convention. For a library you publish, a
D-pointer can preserve binary layout while the implementation evolves. It is useful only when
you make a real binary-compatibility promise.

**Read more:** [Qt object model](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/object.html) and
[KDE binary compatibility](https://community.kde.org/Policies/Binary_Compatibility_Issues_With_C%2B%2B).
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `libs/shapes/`, `src/canvas/`, and `tests/canvas/`
:::
